sources.title: Nanyue King Museum: history exhibition and the Nanyue kingdom
sources.note: Official institutional account, checked through indexed original text; direct retrieval timed out. Territory included present Guangdong, Guangxi and northern Vietnam; founder Zhao Tuo, capital Panyu, Han recognition in 196 BCE, conquest in 111 BCE. The museum uses 203 BCE for foundation; the card marks this approximately because modern chronologies differ. Political value judgments in the exhibition are not adopted.

sources.title: Nanyue King Museum: tomb and palace exhibitions
sources.note: Direct English institutional text checked. Relevant sections only: Nanyue daily utensils, iron tools, Oldest Scripts, Ecology of Panyu, and the curved garden brook. Later Nanhan, Eastern Han and medieval ceramic-pillow sections are excluded. English and Chinese versions of this exhibition are treated as the same underlying work; only this source is budgeted for these claims.

sources.title: Nanyue King Museum: tomb of King Wen of Nanyue
sources.note: Direct Chinese institutional site description checked: discovery in 1983 at Xianggang, identification of the king, seven-chamber plan, sandstone construction and fifteen sacrificial victims. The mode of killing is not specified here and is not invented. No claim that all people of Nanyue shared royal burial customs.

sources.title: State Administration of Cultural Heritage: Site of Southern Yue State, UNESCO Tentative List submission
sources.note: Direct 2008 state-party submission checked, description of palace pond and stone brook, excavated wooden watergate and site coordinates. This is a tentative-list submission, not an inscription on the World Heritage List or an independent UNESCO endorsement. Unsupported global-earliest and modern-engineering-standard superlatives are not repeated.

sources.title: Nanyue King Museum: dragon-knob gold seal of Emperor Wen
sources.note: Indexed original catalogue checked; direct retrieval timed out twice. The face has four incised small-seal-script characters, transcribed by the museum as 文帝行玺. The public sample explicitly uses that modern character rendering. English museum exhibition independently translates the title as Administrative Seal of Emperor Wen. Findspot was the tomb occupant’s chest.

sources.title: Hong Kong Antiquities and Monuments Office: wooden slip, jujube tree No. 94
sources.note: Direct official object record checked. Nanyue-period wooden slip excavated in 2004 at the palace site, collection Nanyue King Museum. English title supplies the meaning jujube tree No. 94. No reconstruction of the Chinese characters is attempted.

sources.title: Nanyue King Museum: bronze roasting stove
sources.note: Full indexed Chinese catalogue checked; direct retrieval timed out. Rectangular bronze stove, 61 cm long, upturned corners, four supports fitted with axle wheels, could be pushed. Found in King Wen’s tomb. Alternate zyzb URL for the same object is not counted as a new work.

sources.title: Nanyue King Museum: bronze textile-printing plates
sources.note: Direct catalogue checked. Two bronze plates used to print designs on silk; matching patterned silk from the western side chamber. Interpretation identifies smaller plate for registration and larger for the principal motif. No claim that the kingdom invented all textile printing.

sources.title: Nanyue King Museum: collections displayed for International Museum Day 2024
sources.note: Full indexed original institutional report checked; direct retrieval timed out. Section on Han Emperor Wu exhibition discusses Nanyue tomb water vessels and ritual hand washing, five-colored medicinal stones and two sets of bronze and iron pounding tools, interpreted in relation to the king’s search for longevity. Medical efficacy is not claimed.

sources.title: Nanyue King Museum: bronze goudiao inscribed with Music Office manufacture
sources.note: Full indexed catalogue checked. Eight instruments, nested at discovery, inscribed Wen Emperor year nine / Music Office manufacture, individually numbered one to eight. Museum converts regnal year nine to 129 BCE. The sample is not used to invent musical notation or the music played.

sources.title: Nanyue King Museum: jade burial suit joined with silk
sources.note: Full indexed Chinese catalogue checked. Suit of 2,291 jade plaques, silk and hemp cloth; drilled and threaded head, hand and foot coverings; reused jade material cut for much of the torso, attached to hemp lining. Royal funerary garment, not ordinary clothing.

sources.title: Nanyue King Museum: gold seal of the Lady of the Right
sources.note: Direct catalogue checked. Four-character title 右夫人玺, turtle-shaped handle with opening for a cord, found in the tomb. The public translation is literal; no reconstruction of her personal biography, household authority or relationship with the king beyond the court title.

sources.title: Nanyue King Museum: silver box
sources.note: Direct catalogue checked. Hammered relief lobes, gilding and an added gilt-bronze foot, with Chinese inscriptions. Catalogue relates the metalworking technique to West Asian traditions. The card does not infer an exact maker, route, direct voyage or migrant household.

sources.title: Nanyue King Museum: four-compartment bronze incense burner
sources.note: Direct catalogue checked. Four separate compartments under a common lid with diamond-shaped openings; silk wrapping traces; tomb incense and comparable Luobowan finds support an elite practice. No medical or universal domestic claim.

sources.title: Vietnam National Museum of History: Vietnam from the first to tenth centuries
sources.note: Original Vietnamese institutional page checked through indexed text; direct retrieval returned cache miss. Explicitly dates Han attack and Trieu collapse to 111 BCE, and emphasizes continued Dong Son traditions evidenced by drums, pottery and bells. The English version drops BCE in its opening; the Vietnamese original is the witness used here.

proposedOverrides.name: Nanyue kingdom
proposedOverrides.summary: Nanyue’s royal capital, practical crafts and written records before Han conquest.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: Independent card for the ancient Nanyue kingdom; no association with medieval Đại Việt or later Nanhan.
batchIdentityNotes.map: Imported circa 200 to 1 BCE; both decoded snapshots have bounds 104.669 to 113.579 east and 18.096 to 22.928 north. Guangzhou palace and tomb are near 23.13 north, so lie beyond the northern edge. This concrete mismatch is public in the overview.
batchIdentityNotes.chronology: Museum chronology begins 203 BCE; foundation given approximately. Conquest in 111 BCE is well supported and represented by an explicit post-conquest period. No geometry alteration or invented founding correction.
batchIdentityNotes.evidenceScope: Most detailed material comes from the royal tomb and palace, not a representative household census. Their provenance and elite setting are kept visible. No contemporary school enrollment or toilet custom established by the consulted sources.
